transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-10-21 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 47m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE); Sanjay Patel (Head Cloud Ops - Hollis); Erin McClellan (CISO - Hollis); Diego Ramos (Product); Priya Singh (Compliance)

Summary: Quick onboarding discovery to understand Hollis constraints around encryption keys, keystore residency, and what logging evidence Redwood can provide for auditors. Customer is a regulated fintech; they want to know whether Redwood Hosted can meet their keystore residency needs or if Dedicated/Private is required.

Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/security-evidence (soc2/iso/keystore-overview), pricing sheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/pricing/hyperscale), private deployment diagram (to be shared).

Action items (recap in call): see metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. Quick round intro?
[00:10] Sanjay: Sanjay here, head of cloud ops at Hollis, thanks for making time.
[00:14] Erin: Erin, CISO. We're primarily here to understand key control and what kind of audit evidence we can get out of Redwood.
[00:18] Diego: Diego, product - I'll be running the POC if we get there.
[00:22] Liam: Great - hi all. To frame the call: we want to map your requirements to the three hosting modes - Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private - and call out keystore and logging implications.
[00:30] Priya: Quick thing: Hollis needs to make sure KMS keys never leave EU control and audit logs must not include full PII. Also legal hold for investigations - retention across regions is a must.
[00:42] Maya: Understood. Maybe start with keystore - are you thinking customer-managed keys in an HSM, or is a cloud-KMS OK if we can restrict locations?
[00:50] Erin: Preference is customer-managed HSM. We need proof of key residency and separation - auditors want to see key control and no Redwood access.
[00:58] Liam: Right - so for Redwood Hosted we offer envelope encryption where customer KMS can be used in certain regions, but there are limits: some model operations (cache encryption/kv cache) may still store ephemeral state on Redwood-managed instances. For true key isolation and no Redwood control over keys, Dedicated or Private is usually the path.
[01:16] Sanjay: When you say "ephemeral state," do you mean anything persistent that could contain PII?
[01:20] Liam: Good question. The runtime writes token metadata and KV cache shards; persistent logs are configurable. We can redact or avoid writing user inputs to logs, but KV cache for performance can include prefixes derived from prompts - that's where we need to discuss minimization.
[01:01] Maya: (laughs) sorry, timestamp drift. To continue: on Hosted we can configure logging minimization and pseudonymization, but auditor comfort varies.
[01:40] Priya: Are you able to run with a customer HSM in our VPC? That's what our legal and risk teams ask for.
[01:47] Liam: For Private deployments yes, you can run an HSM in your network and Redwood's control plane only manages orchestration - keys never leave. For Dedicated, we can do a bring-your-key (BYOK) model where the key is in a cloud KMS with restricted access and we support HSM-backed keys in some regions. There are tradeoffs on autoscaling and maintenance windows.
[02:06] Erin: We need to know: if we go Dedicated and you support HSM-backed keys in the cloud provider, do auditors see evidence that Redwood doesn't have private key material?
[02:16] Liam: We can provide key access logs, KMS audit trails, and a cryptographic boundary description. For Private + customer-managed HSM the material never lands on Redwood controllers. For cloud-KMS we can show KMS CMEK logs showing who invoked Decrypt APIs, timestamps, and principal ids.
[02:30] Sanjay: What about cross-border replication? We operate in both EU and US, but regulated data must remain EU-only for some products.
[02:38] Maya: We support region pinning and model routing. For Hosted we have region options but some model variants are only in certain regions; for strict EU residency we often recommend Dedicated in an EU-only account or Private.
[02:52] Diego: Is there an on-prem pattern where we keep inference inside our data center and Redwood provides orchestration?
[02:58] Liam: Yes - Private includes an on-prem package with a customer-side control plane option. That lets you keep inference and all logs on-prem. The control plane still needs connectivity for updates unless you choose the fully air-gapped package.
[03:14] Priya: Logging: our auditors require that full request payloads are not stored in long-term logs. Can Redwood redact request bodies and only keep metrics?
[03:23] Liam: We have log redaction and sampling. You can configure: no request payloads stored, token-only metrics, and structured telemetry that omits user text. But note: certain debugging modes will capture clipped inputs — those are opt-in.
[03:36] Erin: We also need legal hold; if regulators ask for historical data, how does Redwood handle preservation for a given tenant without exposing other tenants?
[03:45] Maya: For Dedicated/Private we can isolate tenant logs and provide export mechanisms per-tenant. For Hosted we have logical separation and access controls but the underlying storage is multi-tenant; we can provide per-tenant exports and scoped audit logs as evidence.
[03:59] Sanjay: How about redaction quality? We tried a vendor who failed to remove account numbers reliably and that caused a big problem.
[04:07] Liam: Understandable. Our recommended approach is defense-in-depth: client-side masking for PII, plus server-side redaction, and schema-based constraints. For PII that needs to be absolutely never seen by Redwood, encrypt/pseudonymize before calling the model, or run Private on-prem.
[04:25] Diego: Does Redwood support tokenization libraries we can use pre-call?
[04:29] Maya: We have a reference library and patterns in our docs; we'll share the repo link. Also Redwood Optimize can suggest caching/quantization settings that reduce the need to send raw data in many flows.
[04:40] Priya: On auditors: they want to see SOC2 and ISO evidence, and detailed subprocessors list. Can you share that now?
[04:46] Maya: Yes - link in the shared artifacts; we'll also attach a subprocessors CSV in the follow-up.
[04:52] Erin: Another question - model fallbacks and graceful degradation: will logs or traces include prompts when you fallback to a smaller model?
[04:58] Liam: Fallback events are logged. We can redact prompt text and only log model ids, error codes, and token counts. If you prefer no prompt text at all, that's configurable but reduces debug surface.
[05:12] Sanjay: For the POC we'd like to measure KV cache lookup latency and the cost hit of using an HSM vs KMS. Can you run a benchmark with our sample dataset?
[05:20] Liam: Yes, we'll scope a POC. Typical plan: 1) we run KV-cache latency tests on your sample, 2) measure end-to-end RTT using your network egress profile, 3) compare KEK (key-encryption-key) flow added latency for HSM calls. We'll need a target SLA from you to size Dedicated pools if that's the route.
[05:40] Diego: Our target is 150ms p95 for API calls for our credit-check workflow.
[05:45] Liam: Noted. For that SLA we often recommend Dedicated capacity with optimized GPU types and continuous batching; Hosted can get close depending on region and workload. Private/on-prem gives most control but requires ops overhead.
[05:58] Erin: A compliance nuance: we have a subset of data that must be onshore and excluded from backups that replicate to third-country regions. How granular can retention rules be?
[06:07] Maya: We support per-tenant retention policies and route-by-policy. In Dedicated/Private you can set storage locations and disable cross-region replication for specific datasets. Hosted supports route tags and dataset-scoped residency but some low-level backups may still cross regions unless you choose an EU-only Dedicated offering.
[06:25] Priya: Can you produce a diagram showing the keystore flow with calls to KMS/HSM, what is encrypted at rest, and where the ephemeral caches live? Auditors ask for that.
[06:34] Liam: Absolutely — Liam: I'll produce a detailed diagram showing call flows, crypto boundaries, and log redaction points. We'll also annotate which artifacts we can provide as auditor evidence (KMS audit trails, application logs, retention policies).
[06:49] Sanjay: Any third-party subprocessors involved in your runtime? For Hosted we need to map that out for regulators.
[06:55] Maya: We have a subprocessors list; common ones are cloud infra providers, telemetry vendors for SaaS metrics, and our CDN. We'll include versions and contract scopes.
[07:06] Erin: One more - SSO and RBAC: we need SCIM and SAML for provisioning and fine-grained roles so only our security team can request exports.
[07:14] Maya: We support SAML, SCIM, and RBAC with auditing. For Dedicated/Private we can integrate with your IdP directly and sync groups to cluster roles.
[07:24] Diego: If we decide on Private, what is the rough timeline for on-prem provisioning?
[07:29] Liam: For on-prem Private it's typically 6-10 weeks depending on air-gap needs and HSM installation. Dedicated in a single region can be done in 3-4 weeks once contracts are signed. Hosted is immediate.
[07:44] Priya: Cost tradeoffs - HSM is expensive per-op. How do you recommend minimizing HSM calls?
[07:50] Liam: Use hybrid: wrap long-lived DEKs (data encryption keys) with HSM-backed KEKs and cache DEKs in memory with limited TTL. That way runtime does fewer HSM unwraps. We'll show concrete TTL parameters during the POC benchmarking.
[08:06] Sanjay: What about legal hold exports - can we export per-tenant logs without a full backup restore?
[08:11] Maya: Yes; Dedicated/Private support tenant-scoped exports. For Hosted we have APIs to request scoped exports; the process includes verification steps. We can produce attestations of exported datasets for auditors.
[08:25] Erin: Any gotchas with data subject requests (DSR) and deletion? If a user requests deletion, how do you guarantee removal from caches and backups?
[08:34] Liam: We document deletion paths: 1) remove live records, 2) schedule purge of caches (we provide TTL and explicit purge API), 3) backups are on retention cycles but we can perform targeted logical deletes and document the remediation steps. For immutable backups there may be retention windows; we include that in retention policies and can provide a legal justification log.
[08:58] Diego: We're also comparing a competitor who does per-call client-side encryption; how would that affect model features like streaming and tool-calling?
[09:06] Liam: Client-side encryption preserves strong confidentiality but limits model features because the model can't access raw content for tool calls or structured extraction. For streaming you can still stream tokens, but you'd need to decrypt in your environment for post-processing. It's a tradeoff.
[09:22] Maya: To wrap up, we recommend first steps: share your data flow and regulatory list (customer), Redwood will share security evidence and a Private/Dedicated diagram (Redwood), then we'll scope a POC to run KV-cache latency and HSM impact.
[09:36] Priya: Sounds good. Any questions from our side?
[09:39] Sanjay: Not at the moment.
[09:41] Erin: No. Please include an FAQ about what will appear in logs when running in Dedicated vs Hosted.
[09:48] Maya: Will do - we'll include a log-surface FAQ.
[09:52] Diego: Thanks everyone.
[09:54] Maya: Thanks folks — next steps in the calendar invite.

Call end.

Recap (emailed): 1) Redwood to share SOC2/ISO evidence and subprocessors CSV; 2) Redwood SE to deliver keystore flow diagram and POC plan; 3) Customer to send data flow and regulated entity list.
